claims.text: Preheating the build substrate during LPBF of high-entropy alloys reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal gradients minimize residual stresses.
Substrate preheating reduces rapid-cooling-induced microstructural defects.
Reduced residual stress and microstructural defects improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity relative to room-temperature-substrate builds.
Typical room-temperature-substrate LPBF high-entropy-alloy components exhibit residual stress, microcracking, and dimensional deviations.
The proposed intervention is to preheat the build substrate to approximately 600°C during LPBF.
Preheating produces a more homogeneous microstructure with fewer grain-boundary perturbations.
Controlled cooling rates produced by preheating lower residual-stress fields and the density of cracking and porosity.
Preheating permits more controlled solidification by reducing thermal gradients and rapid solidification.
More controlled solidification yields improved dimensional fidelity and mechanical properties.
Relative to room-temperature builds, preheated builds will exhibit less warping and cracking.
Relative to room-temperature builds, preheated builds will exhibit greater dimensional accuracy.
Relative to room-temperature builds, preheated builds will exhibit improved tensile strength and ductility.
Room-temperature-substrate LPBF produces higher thermal gradients, residual stresses, and defect prevalence than preheated-substrate LPBF.
The intervention is expected to apply to high-entropy alloys that tolerate the elevated processing temperature.
Benefits may be limited in thermally unstable alloy systems or when preheating causes performance-degrading grain growth.
Similar substrate-preheating strategies have improved fabrication outcomes in other alloy systems.
The quantitative reduction in defects and improvement in mechanical properties for high-entropy alloys is undetermined.
The proposed experiment compares room-temperature and approximately 600°C substrates while holding other LPBF conditions constant.

The hypothesis is falsified if preheating produces no statistically significant improvement in dimensional accuracy and mechanical integrity and yields comparable or worse defects, residual stress, and mechanical performance.
